newsitem.title: FRANCE: French welfare deficits seen overshooting.
newsitem.headline: French welfare deficits seen overshooting.

text.p: French welfare deficits, a stumbling block in efforts to reduce the state deficit ahead of monetary union, are expected to overshoot targets in 1996 and 1997, the central social security agency ACOSS said on Tuesday.

But economists said they did not think the expected overshoot would threaten significantly France's plans to cut the state deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year in order to qualify for a single European currency in 1999.

An improved outlook for the economy, which many economists now expect to grow more than the 2.3 percent forecast by the government, would cushion public finances from spending slippages, provided these remained small.

An ACOSS official said it estimated the welfare deficit at 54.2 billion francs ($9.6 billion) in 1996, compared to 51.5 billion initially expected. This was partly due to an accounting change which imputed some 1995 spending to the 1996 financial year.
In 1997, the key year for deciding which countries join monetary union, the welfare deficit was expected to reach 35.2 billion francs, compared to 30.4 billion initially forecast.
The ACOSS official said the overshoot was due to a downwards revision in the expected increase in gross wages, seen rising by 2.7 percent instead of 3.3 percent initially expected.

The welfare system, which funds pensions, healthcare and family benefits, is financed mainly through payroll taxes. It has been hit in recent years by unemployment, which has cut the amount of payroll taxes channelled into the system.
Economists said the ACOSS forecast appeared to be on the cautious side and noted that gross wages could in fact likely to rise slightly more than the 2.7 percent now expected.

"The fact that the social security deficit is overshooting probably clomes as very little surprise to people who have been closely following the system," Merrill Lynch economist Joanne Perez said. "If the overshoot can be held at five billion francs I think that's already not bad," she added.
ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said the revised welfare figures were fairly good overall.

In previous years, the welfare system ran up deeper deficits of some 60 billion francs a year. The government has since implemented spending curbs and floated off the system's debts into a separate body to lift the burden of debt-service charges.
The total state deficit covers the central government, welfare, unemployment and local authority spending. The government has estimated it at 4.1 percent of GDP in 1996.

Economists said they remained confident France would reduce the state deficit to or near three percent of GDP this year, even outshining Germany, whose image as Europe's model economy has been tarnished by its own problems in reducing its deficit.
"I personally think that within 0.1 to 0.2 percent, France will be very close to target -- much closer than Germany and that for us is where the real problem lies," Perez said.
A range of indicators pointing to an improved economic outlook should also help France this year.

"There is a growing sensation that life is not so black in France as it is in Germany," Credit Lyonnais economist Iain Lindsay said. "France has got that cushion of flexibility inbuilt which Germany does not seem to have at all.

Despite Germany's troubles, most expect France to go all out to make sure that it will meet the three percent target, to strengthen its negotiating hand when European Union leaders agree in early 1998 which countries qualify for monetary union.
"They want to be absolutely certain they will meet three percent," Brossard said.
